Pierre points to the phone calls listed under the coffee shop's recurring window. "The draft is polite." Everly nods. "Then send the invite, not the applause."
examples.whatToDo: Pierre should replace the saved praise with a short invitation to talk during the window he has already made easy to use.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange keeps the lesson inside the reply itself. Praise can be kind, but an invitation creates room for the other person to answer.

examples.title: Feed Pause
examples.scenario: Everly sits this afternoon at the east concourse gate with a boarding pass on her knee. Facebook is open, and the Like button waits under a friend's promotion news. She thinks, If I tap, I was there. Then another thought follows: if I tap, I will check who tapped mine. The one-click reaction teaches her which social acknowledgement to crave.
examples.whatToDo: Everly should close the feed and send one direct sentence later: she saw the news and wants to hear the story when the friend has time.
examples.whyItMatters: The pause exposes the reward loop from the inside. Giving weak signals can train the same hunger that makes receiving them feel urgent.

questions.prompt: A volunteer group wants to cut social media use, but one member worries the rule treats friendship as shallow. Which reply best fits the starting point?
choices: The group should mute the worry so members stop defending old habits in public.
The group should keep every channel open because social need outweighs planned limits.
The group should honor the need for connection while changing the weak substitutes.
questions.explanation: The critique begins by accepting social need as real. The target is substitution by weak signals, not friendship itself, so suppression and total openness both miss the mechanism.

questions.prompt: Melanie tells Sabrina, "I liked five posts from my old roommate this week, so I have been a good friend." What does this claim miss?
choices: The roommate may prefer private comments because public reactions look casual.
The posts may need longer comments because the platform ranks those higher.
The likes may satisfy acknowledgement without creating conversation or understanding.
questions.explanation: A Like can feel like reaching out because it is easy and public. More acknowledgement is not the same as deeper contact, which is the near-miss in the claim.

questions.prompt: During a family conflict, Danielle suggests moving from texts to a call. Which reason best matches Sherry Turkle's conversation standard?
choices: A call asks people to hear tone, wait, respond, and repair what lands badly.
A call records fewer words, so each person can avoid overexplaining the conflict.
A call moves faster, so the family can finish the hard topic with less effort.
questions.explanation: Turkle's standard is richer interaction: listening, timing, ambiguity, and response. The wrong choices treat the call as a shortcut, not as harder social work.

questions.prompt: At dinner, Gerald says a cousin keeps six chats active all day and has not made one call in months. What is the most likely social cost?
choices: The chats may make logistics harder because everyone expects formal planning.
The chats may keep the bond superficially active while crowding out deeper contact.
The chats may prove the relationship is strong because attention arrives all day.
questions.explanation: Constant texting can maintain a low-grade sense of contact. That can reduce the push to schedule calls, visits, or longer exchanges where the friendship deepens.

questions.prompt: Brynn posts that Friday evenings are open for coffee, walks, or calls. Which outcome would show the office-hours idea working?
choices: Friends know when real conversation is welcome, so Brynn can stop monitoring every ping.
Friends send fewer serious messages during the week, so Brynn can avoid awkward topics more politely.
Friends compete for the Friday window, so Brynn can measure which relationships matter most.
questions.explanation: Conversation office hours concentrate availability. They are not avoidance or ranking; they make richer contact easier while reducing all-day reactivity.

questions.prompt: Everly stops giving quick reactions for a week after noticing she checks her own posts for hearts. Beyond the platform's metrics, what personal habit might change?
choices: She may need to post more often because fewer reactions make her less visible.
She may care less about visible reactions because she is no longer training on them.
She may lose track of friends because reactions are the fastest way to notice their news.
questions.explanation: Giving and receiving visible reactions trains attention toward the reward loop. Opting out changes what Everly teaches herself to value.

questions.prompt: During a planning call, Pierre says, "A short comment under a post is basically the same as a walk." Which distinction should correct him?
choices: The comment is better when it is public, while the walk is better when it stays private.
The comment is useful only for logistics, while the walk is useful only for emotion.
The walk carries tone, pacing, context, and commitment that a quick comment lacks.
questions.explanation: High-bandwidth contact carries more social information. A comment can be friendly, but it lacks much of the shared context and attention of a walk.

questions.prompt: When Pierre reads a friend's hard update, he refuses to click Like and instead schedules a visit. What does that choice show?
choices: He is making care less visible so the relationship carries fewer social demands.
He is moving care from weak acknowledgement toward stronger presence.
He is proving that online signals damage every relationship that uses them.
questions.explanation: The goal is social upgrade, not withdrawal. Pierre reduces a weak signal so he can spend more effort on a visit, which is stronger presence.

questions.prompt: A parent uses texts to coordinate pickup times, then expects the same thread to carry a hard talk with a teenager. What should change?
choices: Keep the texts for coordination and move the emotional talk to voice or shared time.
Make the thread longer so the teenager has more written detail to review after pickup later.
Treat the useful pickup texts as proof that texting can handle closeness too.
questions.explanation: Digital minimalism separates jobs. Texting can be excellent for logistics, but closeness usually needs a richer channel than the coordination thread.

reviewCards.front: What does conversation-centric connection ask you to treat as the main form of relationship care?
reviewCards.back: Treat voice, face, and sustained exchange as the main care channels. Likes, reactions, and quick texts can support a bond, but they should not replace calls, visits, walks, or real-time talk.

reviewCards.front: Why can a Like feel social while still weakening the next real contact?
reviewCards.back: A Like lets you feel that you noticed someone with almost no effort. That feeling can close the mental loop before you call, ask a follow-up, or spend time with the person.

reviewCards.front: How does Sherry Turkle's conversation standard explain why empathy needs more than snippets?
reviewCards.back: Conversation makes people listen, wait, read tone, respond, and repair. Those demands train empathy in a way that short comments and reactions do not.

reviewCards.front: What problem do conversation office hours solve?
reviewCards.back: They make real contact predictable. Friends know when calls, walks, or visits are welcome, so you can stop being loosely available to every ping all day.

reviewCards.front: How should texting and conversation divide the work of friendship?
reviewCards.back: Use texting for coordination, such as times, places, and quick facts. Use calls, meals, walks, and face-to-face talk for the parts that need tone, attention, and depth.

reviewCards.front: Recall digital declutter (Ch 3): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Brynn's Friday coffee-shop window shows the declutter idea in action. She replaces all-day thread checking with a chosen rule for richer contact, rather than leaving empty space.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice naming the channel that would carry care best before you react. The move is simple: pause at the next social prompt, say the stronger channel aloud, then use the tiny signal only if it supports that channel. This keeps logistics useful and keeps friendship from shrinking to visible clicks.

ifThenPlans.context: If a Like button feels like the whole reply to someone you care about
ifThenPlans.plan: If the click would end your effort, then say the stronger channel aloud and send a short invite to talk instead.

ifThenPlans.context: If a text thread has stayed busy for days without one real exchange
ifThenPlans.plan: If the thread is only keeping the bond warm, then say the stronger channel aloud and offer one call or walk.

ifThenPlans.context: If friends expect quick replies from you all day
ifThenPlans.plan: If constant replies are thinning your attention, then say the stronger channel aloud and name a recurring window for calls or visits.

ifThenPlans.context: If a logistical text turns into a serious emotional topic
ifThenPlans.plan: If coordination has become care, then say the stronger channel aloud and move the hard part to voice or shared time.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, before you start your next social message thread, say one sentence aloud: "This needs a stronger channel." Then choose call, walk, visit, or logistics-only text.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, run a swap experiment: replace one recurring Like or quick-reply habit with one spoken invitation. Compare the two halves by how much real exchange each produced.

memorableLines.text: A Like is not care; it is a receipt.
A ping can arrange a walk, but it cannot take the walk for you.
Weak signals are fine as sparks; they fail as meals.

chapters.title: Reclaim Leisure
chapters.hook: Which hobby would you still choose if it felt clumsy for the first week?
chapters.counterintuition: Why does leisure that asks more from you often leave you steadier afterward? Because the effort is not a tax on the fun; it is part of how the fun gets deep enough to last.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next conversation about free time, move one hobby object into view and explain how it could make a hard first step easier than opening a feed.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Reclaimed time stays reclaimed when you fill it with active leisure that takes setup, skill, people, or tools, then keep passive screens in a small planned box.

breakdown.fastRead: Daphne finds a free hour after dinner and notices how strange it feels to protect it. Arnold Bennett would have treated that hour as raw material, not leftover scraps. His reversal is simple: demanding activity can be better leisure than passive consumption. A bike ride, a repair, a club night, or a hard book may resist you at first. Easy fun fades when it asks nothing of you. The rule is not to turn rest into work. It is to give your free hours something strong enough to compete with the easiest screen in the room.
breakdown.deepRead: The mechanism is visible the moment the first obstacle appears. High-quality leisure has startup friction: the cold garage, the awkward first meeting, the out-of-tune guitar, the recipe that dirties three pans. A feed has almost none. That is why empty time slides toward it unless you give the hour another destination. Pete Adeney's Mr. Money Mustache world makes the point in a lively way. Bryan rolls a bike wheel across the garage while Delaney asks why anyone with a car would bother fixing spokes on a Saturday. Bryan says the ride is cheaper, yes, but the bigger reward is that his body and hands know how the afternoon was spent. Frugality stops feeling like a smaller life when biking, repair, and local competence make the day feel fuller. Hands remember progress before feeds do. This is also why social leisure matters. A club, game night, volunteer shift, or pickup match gives connection a shape. You do not have to maintain every weak tie through a platform when a few strong ties have a place to meet. The discrimination is practical: if an activity only fills time, it is fragile; if it builds skill, contact, service, or shared effort, it can hold the space your phone used to occupy.
breakdown.fullRead:
Matthew Crawford's shop work adds a sharper edge: tools answer back. A motorcycle part either fits or it does not. A wooden joint either sits square or it wobbles. That concrete feedback can feel humbling, but it also gives agency back to the person doing the work. Screens often blur that line. You scroll, react, compare, and receive little clean evidence that you made anything better. Manual competence is not valuable only because it saves money. It gives the mind a real object, a standard, and a visible result.

Drew learns this while helping Adeline fix a loose brake cable. The first ten minutes are all fumbling: wrong wrench, dropped bolt, grease on the towel. Then the cable tightens, the lever responds, and the bike becomes rideable again. Nobody would call those ten minutes effortless. They are satisfying because they were not effortless. The body knows the difference between being entertained and having done something.

Planning matters because good leisure rarely appears fully formed. You may need to buy the cheap tool, text the group, reserve the court, choose a hard book, or put the guitar where your hand will find it. That sounds less spontaneous than collapsing onto the couch, but it is often what lets real delight happen. Structure can protect play. When low-quality digital leisure stays unplanned, it becomes the default answer to every pause. When it is scheduled into a small window, it can stay a treat instead of becoming the shape of the day.

The planning should stay light enough to invite action. A reader does not need a full hobby curriculum before touching a tool. One visible object can be enough: the racket by the door, the library novel on the pillow, the bike pump beside the wheel. The object matters because it changes the first move. Instead of asking, "What do I feel like doing?" while a phone waits nearby, the room answers with a small prepared path. The path can still be playful. Friends can still improvise after the first serve, and a repair can still turn into a long talk over coffee.

There is still a counter-case. If Laurence comes home sick, child asleep at last, and a simple show helps him recover without crowding out anything better, the Bennett Principle should not scold him into building a bookshelf. Passive comfort can be honest rest when it is chosen, contained, and not covering an avoided life. A screen can rest you; it cannot replace a life. Reclaiming leisure means knowing the difference between a planned comfort and the kind of passive drift that quietly spends every open hour.

examples.title: Bennett's Free Hour
examples.scenario: Daphne leaves a printed note about Arnold Bennett on the kitchen table: early twentieth century, free hours, demanding activity. Bryan points to the couch and says she has earned an easy show. Daphne weighs two poor options: collapse into another night of passive consumption, or start the sketchbook practice that will feel clumsy for ten minutes before it feels alive.
examples.whatToDo: Daphne puts the remote in a drawer, leaves the sketchbook open beside Bennett's note, and asks Bryan to stay for the first page instead of praising the plan from across the room.
examples.whyItMatters: The move makes the first hard step visible and shared. When leisure has startup friction, a prepared object and one witness can keep the hour from sliding back to the easiest screen.

examples.title: Garage Spoke Talk
examples.scenario: At noon on the shop floor in Bryan's garage, bike mechanic Bryan spins a wobbly wheel beside a workbench and a mug of cold coffee. "Why not just drive?" Delaney asks. Bryan points to the Mr. Money Mustache post about Pete Adeney, financial independence, biking and repair. "Because this is not only about saving gas," he says. "I get a ride, a fixed wheel, and an afternoon I can feel in my legs."
examples.whatToDo: Bryan keeps the talk at the workbench. He lets Delaney hold the spoke key, names the repair step, and turns financial independence from a spreadsheet into a lived action.
examples.whyItMatters: The exchange turns less consumption into more agency. A reader can copy the pattern by pairing restraint with a body-level skill, not with a vague promise to spend less.

examples.title: The Bolt Answers
examples.scenario: At the Saturday shop bench, Delaney expects the motorcycle repair to be a noble waste of time. A mechanic reads a marked page from Matthew Crawford's Shop Class as Soulcraft, then asks her to tighten one bolt on the stand. The surprise comes when the part stops rattling. "That was the whole point?" she asks. The mechanic smiles: "The metal answered you."
examples.whatToDo: Delaney repeats the adjustment herself and listens for the rattle to disappear. She lets the tool give feedback before judging the repair by speed or savings.
examples.whyItMatters: Manual skill teaches through reality, not through likes or guesses. The reader learns to value a hobby that gives clear standards even when it starts slowly.

examples.title: Pickup Game Thread
examples.scenario: Friday group text, 11:18 a.m. Holden: "Pete Adeney's Mr. Money Mustache crowd would bike to the court, right?" Adeline: "Only if we actually meet instead of liking photos." Holden: "I have not played in a year." Adeline: "Good. Biking and repair can wait. Today we can be bad in person." By noon, the chat has become two borrowed rackets and a tennis court gate.
examples.whatToDo: Adeline turns the weak online signal into a shared appointment. She names a place, lowers the skill bar, and makes the connection happen through play.
examples.whyItMatters: Structured leisure gives friendship a body and a calendar. It does not require constant platform upkeep because people know when and where to meet.

examples.title: Remote In The Bowl
examples.scenario: After bedtime in the apartment hallway, Laurence starts the third episode with a baby monitor in one hand and the remote in the other. Drew taps the Arnold Bennett note on the table: free hours, demanding activity. "Are we resting, or did the remote win again?" Laurence pauses the show, carries the remote to a bowl by the door, and says one episode can stay.
examples.whatToDo: Laurence restarts the night with a rule he can see. He places the remote away from his hand, names the one planned episode, and pulls out the puzzle box for after.
examples.whyItMatters: The reset does not treat every show as failure. It keeps passive leisure inside a chosen window so it cannot quietly become the answer to every gap.

examples.title: Grease On The Towel
examples.scenario: At the workbench, Adeline holds the brake cable while a neighbor wipes grease from a towel already ruined for the purpose. Matthew Crawford's motorcycle repair pages sit open nearby, but the lesson is in the lever. Adeline squeezes; the brake grabs cleanly. "It finally listens," the neighbor says, and she grins at the small, physical proof.
examples.whatToDo: Adeline stays with the awkward part until the feedback changes. She tests the lever again, cleans the tool, and treats the finished motion as the reward.
examples.whyItMatters: Startup friction is not a sign to quit. Skilled leisure often becomes satisfying only after the hand, tool, and material begin to answer one another.

questions.prompt: "I deleted the apps, so better hobbies should show up on their own." What does this response miss?
choices: It treats free hours as proof that discipline has already replaced entertainment.
It leaves empty time exposed to easy digital entertainment before better leisure is ready.
It assumes every screen habit should be replaced by the same outdoor activity.
questions.explanation: The source fact says reclaimed time needs satisfying replacements. The first choice overstates discipline, and the third narrows leisure to one category.

questions.prompt: A reader says a relaxing night should demand as little as possible. Which reply best fits the Bennett Principle?
choices: Demanding activity can produce stronger satisfaction because skill and effort are part of the reward.
Passive activity is useful only when it trains a person to work harder the next day.
A restful night should be judged by whether it avoids tools, groups, and practice.
questions.explanation: Bennett favors demanding activity over passive consumption. The other choices either make rest serve work or treat friction as automatic evidence against leisure.

questions.prompt: After trying to replace scrolling, Holden chooses only running. What is the likely blind spot?
choices: High-quality leisure can also include craft, music, clubs, repair, reading, or service.
Outdoor exercise matters less than private digital rules for long-term attention.
Any activity counts as high-quality leisure once it happens away from a phone.
questions.explanation: The fact names active engagement across several forms, not only exercise. The other choices either leave the source focus or make the standard too loose.

questions.prompt: Someone calls Mr. Money Mustache a lesson in spreadsheets and self-denial. What is the better reading?
choices: The example links lower consumption with biking, repair, and competence that make life feel richer.
The example proves financial independence works when leisure is postponed until savings are complete.
The example treats frugality as a private accounting method with little effect on daily life.
questions.explanation: Pete Adeney's case pairs frugality with active competence. The distractors flatten the example into deferred pleasure or accounting alone.

questions.prompt: "Repair hobbies are worth it because they save cash." What does Crawford's manual-competence argument add?
choices: Repair matters when it turns every free hour into a practical job with measurable output.
Repair matters when it keeps entertainment away until useful chores are finished.
Repair gives concrete feedback from tools and materials, which restores agency.
questions.explanation: Crawford's point is agency through contact with reality. The other choices reduce craft to productivity or delayed entertainment.

questions.prompt: A group quits the platform chat but never sets a shared activity. What is most likely to happen next?
choices: The friendship improves because less ambient contact leaves more room for stronger bonds.
The group avoids digital upkeep while keeping all the benefits of regular presence.
Connection weakens unless a club, game, volunteer shift, or gathering gives it structure.
questions.explanation: The fact says structured shared activity carries connection better than ambient contact. Less online chatter alone does not create a meeting place.

questions.prompt: "A minimalist should never stream shows or browse for fun." Which correction fits the method?
choices: Passive entertainment is acceptable only after all demanding leisure has become easy.
Passive entertainment can stay as a planned treat, but it should not fill every gap by default.
Passive entertainment should be replaced by social platforms that feel more active.
questions.explanation: The source allows contained low-quality leisure. The first choice invents an ease test, and the third swaps one screen default for another.

questions.prompt: Daphne's first guitar session feels awkward and tiring. What should she infer from the idea?
choices: The hobby is probably mismatched because good leisure should relax her at once.
The hobby should be kept only if it quickly becomes cheaper than screen entertainment.
The awkward start may be normal friction before the activity becomes rewarding.
questions.explanation: Fact 8 warns against reading startup friction as failure. The distractors expect instant ease or reduce the choice to price.

questions.prompt: A team removes casual browsing but refuses to plan leisure because planning sounds joyless. What follows from the source logic?
choices: Spontaneity works best when every free block stays open until the last moment.
Some structure gives reclaimed time a positive destination without killing play.
Planning matters only for work because leisure loses value once it is named.
questions.explanation: The fact says planning protects the declutter from becoming a void. The other choices repeat the error that structure ruins leisure.

reviewCards.front: What makes leisure high quality in a digital minimalist life?
reviewCards.back: It asks for active engagement: skill, tools, movement, service, study, or shared effort. The test is whether the activity gives deeper satisfaction than passive digital consumption.

reviewCards.front: How does the Bennett Principle reverse the usual idea of rest?
reviewCards.back: It says demanding activity can be better leisure than passive ease. Effort, practice, and skill are not defects; they are often what make the reward durable.

reviewCards.front: Why should startup friction not automatically disqualify a hobby?
reviewCards.back: Many good activities begin with setup, awkwardness, weak skill, or tired muscles. That early drag can be the entry cost for satisfaction that lasts.

reviewCards.front: What does Pete Adeney's Mr. Money Mustache example add to leisure?
reviewCards.back: It shows reduced consumption becoming richer through biking, repair, and local competence. Frugality feels less like deprivation when daily life gets more active.

reviewCards.front: Why does Matthew Crawford matter for a chapter about screens?
reviewCards.back: His manual-competence argument shows why making and fixing restore agency. Tools and materials give feedback that passive information rarely provides.

reviewCards.front: Which matters more for reclaimed free time, digital minimalism (Ch 2) or high-quality leisure, and why?
reviewCards.back: Digital minimalism decides which tools deserve a place. High-quality leisure keeps the freed time from becoming empty, so the replacement activity carries the practical burden.

reviewCards.front: Does the method ban low-quality digital leisure?
reviewCards.back: No. It contains passive entertainment in planned windows so it stays a treat. The target is default drift, not every movie, show, or casual browse.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice giving reclaimed time a visible destination before the easy screen claims it. Use the Place the Harder Fun move: put one tool, book, racket, recipe, or invitation where the next leisure moment will begin. Then treat early friction as a cue to start smaller, not as proof the activity is wrong.

ifThenPlans.context: An open evening appears after you reduce a screen habit.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the hour feels empty, then choose the prepared object before choosing entertainment. Give the activity ten minutes before you judge it.

ifThenPlans.context: A hobby feels awkward during the first session.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the first attempt feels clumsy, then name the friction out loud and make the next step smaller. Do not let awkwardness vote by itself.

ifThenPlans.context: You catch yourself relying on feed contact with friends.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a relationship is living mostly in reactions and likes, then propose one shared activity with a place and a day.

ifThenPlans.context: You want a show, game, or browsing session.
ifThenPlans.plan: If passive entertainment is the choice, then put it in a clear window first. Stop when the window ends and move the remote, controller, or app away.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: In the next 24 hours, move one leisure object into the spot where you usually reach for a screen. During your next conversation about free time, explain to one person why that object marks your first ten minutes.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, teach the Bennett Principle to one person in plain language using your real leisure plan. Show the object you moved, name the first friction point, and ask them what would make the start easier.

memorableLines.text: Easy fun fades when it asks nothing of you.
Hands remember progress before feeds do.
A screen can rest you; it cannot replace a life.

chapters.title: Join the Attention Resistance
chapters.hook: Your lock screen is not neutral; it quietly votes before your values speak.
chapters.counterintuition: Resistance is not a one-time deletion, but a steady redesign of the paths your attention can take. If the feed keeps the easiest door, your best values wait outside it.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next commute or first coffee, count each reflex pull toward a feed. Record the cue, the app, and rank the top three by risk to your attention.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Attention resistance protects autonomy by making chosen tools easy and captured use hard: remove phone feeds, slow your news, and add friction where defaults keep winning.

breakdown.fastRead:
Jaron Lanier gives the hard version of the move. In Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now, he treats exit as a sane answer to surveillance and behavior manipulation, not as a stunt. A platform can help you and still be built to pull you back. Defaults vote before you do.

Your job is to make the vote harder to cast. Remove social apps from the phone. Read news from selected sources after the rush has cooled. Use a platform with a purpose, a time, and a clean exit. The aim is not to hate tools. The aim is to keep your own hand on the switch.
breakdown.deepRead:
Platforms win when return visits feel like your idea. A buzz, a badge, a new post, or a red dot can turn a free minute into a measured act. Tristan Harris and the Center for Humane Technology named this as a design problem. Time Well Spent was a way to ask what a screen was steering people toward before they had chosen it.

That is why rules beat mood. If Thomas keeps the account but removes the app, the account has not vanished. The thumb path has changed. A check now asks for a laptop, a browser, and a reason. That small delay gives his values a chance to speak.

Slow media works the same way with news. Solene can still care about the world without letting breaking news own the shape of her day. She picks selected sources, waits for context, and reads when she can think. Speed is not the same as care. Friction is a fence around chosen attention.

The full tactic set has five parts: delete or exit corrosive platforms, remove social media from phones, use social media like a professional, embrace slow media, and use friction tools and single-purpose devices. Each part asks the same plain question: who decides what gets the next minute?
breakdown.fullRead:
A dumb phone on the table can look pure while the laptop across the room still holds every feed. That is the danger of turning resistance into a costume. The plain phone is only a tool, not proof. Ask a plainer thing: does the easiest path still lead where you chose?

Jaron Lanier's exit case matters because some platforms mix surveillance, behavior manipulation, and public talk in ways a careful user may not be able to tame. Leaving can be rational. It is not the only honest answer. A freelance designer may need one network to find clients. A school volunteer may need a group page to post dates. Resistance asks them to write rules sharp enough that the tool works for the job and then goes quiet.

Treating a platform as a work tool gives that rule a shape. Pierce names the purpose before opening the site. He writes the session length. He writes what success looks like. Then he leaves when the job is done. Without those marks, the session can become wandering with better shoes.

Tristan Harris adds the design warning. A feed, a notification, and a metric are not just taste choices. They steer behavior before a person can weigh the trade. That means the repair must reach the setting, not just the mood. Blockers, grayscale, separate devices, and single-purpose work tools are not signs of weak will. They are rails laid for the self you already chose.

Murray's team shows the small version. No one throws a phone into the sea. They turn noisy internal posts into a summary, keep safety alerts, and make the feed serve one work path. The change is modest enough to last. It also proves the larger rule: change the room before you blame the mind.

Slow media protects another edge. Constant headline checks can feel like duty, but duty without context often becomes noise. Solene waits for selected sources and delayed reading. She misses some heat and gains a clearer picture. A person can be later than the feed and wiser than the feed.

Push the idea too far and it curdles. Purity can become another feed. You start checking whether you are austere enough, clean enough, severe enough. That is still attention captured by a display, only now the display is your own rule sheet. The goal is autonomy, not a museum of unused tools. Keep the tools that serve a chosen value. Make the captured uses harder. Then keep watching, because new defaults will keep asking for the next minute.

examples.title: Lanier Lunch Correction
examples.scenario: At noon Thomas types in the hospital cafeteria while his soup cools. He works as a patient advocate, and his lunch reply defends his social accounts as harmless. Jaron Lanier's Ten Arguments for Deleting Your Social Media Accounts Right Now sits beside the bowl. Thomas notices his own error: he has judged only the nice posts, not the surveillance and behavior manipulation that pay for the feed. The reply box is still open, and he can admit the account may need an exit.
examples.whatToDo: Thomas sends the shorter honest reply: the account is useful sometimes, but its business model keeps winning his spare minutes. He deletes one corrosive account before lunch ends.
examples.whyItMatters: The recovery happens at the moment of noticing. When the platform's incentives are the problem, more willpower inside the same feed may be weaker than leaving it.

examples.title: Pierce's Default Memo
examples.scenario: Pierce's memo opens on a projector before the town hall: "Tristan Harris and the Center for Humane Technology make this more than taste. Our default alert asks for attention before the user has a task. Time Well Spent would judge the path we create, not the color we pick." In the final line, he recommends changing the default from instant alerts to quiet summaries.
examples.whatToDo: Pierce keeps the memo concrete: name the default, state what it asks from the user, and recommend the quieter setting before anyone can wave it off as a design preference.
examples.whyItMatters: Written this way, the choice becomes ethical and practical. Defaults are part of the environment, so changing them protects attention before discipline is tested.

examples.title: Two News Mornings
examples.scenario: At 7:35 a.m. Gaelle refreshes breaking news in a rideshare back seat before the car clears the bridge. She works as a public-interest attorney and arrives with fragments and a tight jaw. Solene works as a policy analyst. She waits until lunch, reads two selected sources, and writes three lines of context in a notebook. Gaelle feels earlier; Solene can explain more. The same story leaves one person stirred and the other informed.
examples.whatToDo: Solene keeps the selected sources and delayed reading window. Gaelle changes one variable tomorrow: no headline refresh during the ride, only one chosen source after the morning rush.
examples.whyItMatters: Slow media does not mean caring less. It trades speed and frequency for context, so the reader can notice when checking is feeding nerves more than knowledge.

examples.title: Murray's Feed Reframe
examples.scenario: Murray walks the factory floor with a tablet that pings for every internal post. Renata, the peer coach, taps the notification list and brings up Tristan Harris's warning about interface defaults. "Do not call it weak focus when the room keeps handing people a bell," she says. Murray stops blaming the crew and asks which alerts can become scheduled summaries.
examples.whatToDo: Murray changes the environment first: convert nonurgent pings into summaries, leave safety alerts alone, and make the feed a work tool with a clear entry point.
examples.whyItMatters: The coach talk moves the problem from character to design. When the setting keeps calling, friction is not a crutch; it is part of the work.

examples.title: Tracy's Professional Session
examples.scenario: Tracy stands in a community college lab after showing a short Tristan Harris clip from the Center for Humane Technology. New club officers plan social posts. One student says attention resistance means better photos and more frequent updates. Tracy writes three blanks on the board: purpose, schedule, exit. The confusion becomes the lesson. A platform can serve the club, but only if the session ends when the announcement, reply, or sign-up check is done.
examples.whatToDo: Tracy has each officer write one purpose, one session window, and one success mark before logging in. The class treats the feed as a tool, not a room to roam.
examples.whyItMatters: The teaching case separates polish from control. Professional use is not about looking busier online; it is about ending the session when the defined job is complete.

examples.title: Gaelle's Missing App
examples.scenario: On Saturday Gaelle waits in the apartment laundry room while the washer shakes. She works as a public-interest attorney and used to check a feed between loads. After hearing Tristan Harris on interface defaults, she removed the phone app. The account stayed open, but the missing icon changes the urge. Fetching a laptop feels like a choice. Most times she folds towels instead; later she logs in for one message and leaves.
examples.whatToDo: Gaelle leaves the account active but removes the easiest path. She uses the desktop only for named tasks, then signs out before the feed becomes the next room she lives in.
examples.whyItMatters: The before-and-after shows why friction matters. Deleting the app can change the behavior even when the account still exists.

questions.prompt: During a vendor demo, Murray hears, "The platform wants users to get value quickly, so more checking is still their choice." What does this miss?
choices: It assumes reminders can be turned off without changing the platform's business incentives.
It misses that captured time and behavior data can reward extra checking beyond the user's aim.
It treats every ad-funded tool as useless even when a narrow task still has value.
questions.explanation: The conflict is not only the user's intent. Platforms can gain from extra return visits, while the first and third choices shift the issue to settings or total rejection.

questions.prompt: Thomas reads Lanier and says, "If deletion is serious, every minimalist must delete every account." Which reply fits the case best?
choices: Deletion is mainly a public signal, so Thomas should keep accounts and post less.
Deletion matters only after Thomas proves that every constrained-use rule failed first.
Deletion can be a rational exit when surveillance and manipulation defeat autonomy.
questions.explanation: Lanier's argument supports exit as one strong strategy, not a universal rule. The other choices either reduce exit to image or make it a last resort only.

questions.prompt: Before Pierce's town hall, his team calls an instant-alert default "just a style preference." Which response follows humane technology thinking?
choices: The team should poll users about color and placement before judging the alert.
The team should keep the alert if most workers say they like fast updates.
The team should ask how the default steers behavior before choice can catch up.
questions.explanation: Harris's work treats defaults as ethical design choices because they shape behavior. Taste and user preference matter, but they do not settle the steering effect.

questions.prompt: Gaelle keeps her social account but deletes the phone app. A friend says nothing has changed. Which result is most likely?
choices: Gaelle will need a stricter promise because active accounts make friction useless.
Gaelle will check with the same rhythm because the account still exists online.
Gaelle will face a small delay that turns reflex checks into more chosen sessions.
questions.explanation: The account remains, but the easy access path is gone. That friction can interrupt automatic checking, while the other choices treat app removal as empty.

questions.prompt: In Tracy's club workshop, officers need social media for event notices but keep drifting into the feed. What would professional use require?
choices: Tracy defines the purpose, opens the site in a set window, and leaves when the notice is done.
Tracy improves the club's photos and posts more often so the account looks active.
Tracy keeps the account open between classes so replies can be handled as they arrive.
questions.explanation: Professional use means a purpose, schedule, and exit condition. Better polish or constant availability can still leave the session open to wandering.

questions.prompt: In the rideshare, Gaelle worries that delayed news reading will make her careless about the world. Which answer best reflects slow media?
choices: Gaelle should scan headlines all day but avoid opening most articles.
Gaelle can use selected sources later, gaining context while losing some heat.
Gaelle should wait for friends to summarize news so she avoids anxious reading.
questions.explanation: Slow media reduces speed and frequency to improve context. It is not headline skimming all day, and it is not outsourcing attention to friends.

questions.prompt: On Murray's factory floor, a colleague calls blockers and single-purpose devices "training wheels." Which reply best fits attention resistance?
choices: They reshape the environment so the chosen action is easier when willpower is low.
They prove the user should leave every platform rather than keep making rules.
They work mainly by making devices unpleasant enough that work feels better.
questions.explanation: Friction tools align the setting with the desired behavior. The other choices confuse design support with total exit or with making technology feel bad.

questions.prompt: After Solene finishes a digital declutter, she says attention should stay fixed now. What is the weak spot in that claim?
choices: New defaults and old habits can return, so rules need review and repair.
A declutter only works when every social account is deleted at the end.
A reset mainly measures discipline, so later tool choices matter much less.
questions.explanation: Attention resistance is ongoing. A declutter can reset habits, but platforms and routines keep changing, so the defenses need upkeep.

questions.prompt: Solene wants to join the attention resistance without becoming anti-technology or performative. Which rule best matches the goal?
choices: Solene should remove tools until her setup proves she is no longer tempted by feeds.
Solene should keep useful tools only where she sets the purpose, path, and stopping point.
Solene should treat modern platforms as acceptable whenever they help with a real task.
questions.explanation: The goal is autonomy, not purity. Useful tools may remain, but the user sets terms. The other choices lean toward image or loose permission.

reviewCards.front: What does attention resistance ask you to resist?
reviewCards.back: It asks you to resist letting feeds, alerts, platforms, and devices set the terms for your attention. You change the paths so chosen uses are easier than captured ones.

reviewCards.front: When does Lanier's deletion argument become a rational exit rather than a stunt?
reviewCards.back: Deletion makes sense when surveillance, behavior manipulation, and public-discourse harms are built into the platform's incentives. In that case, leaving can protect autonomy.

reviewCards.front: Why do Tristan Harris and humane technology treat defaults as ethical choices?
reviewCards.back: Interface defaults can invite a check before a person has named a task. Center for Humane Technology used Time Well Spent to judge that steering, not just screen style.

reviewCards.front: How does slow media make someone better informed with fewer checks?
reviewCards.back: It trades breaking news checks for selected sources and scheduled reading. Delayed consumption lets noise fade before attention is spent, so context has room to form.

reviewCards.front: What three marks make social media use professional rather than wandering?
reviewCards.back: Professional use has a purpose, a schedule, and an exit condition. The session starts with a job and ends when that job is done.

reviewCards.front: How would you restate conversation-centric connection (Ch 5), then use it on attention resistance?
reviewCards.back: Conversation-centric connection makes voice, face, and sustained exchange the main form of care. Attention resistance protects those channels without turning useful tools into forbidden objects.

reviewCards.front: Why is autonomy a better target than technological purity?
reviewCards.back: Purity can become image management. Autonomy asks who controls attention, so selected tools may stay when the user sets the purpose, path, and stopping point.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice spotting the easiest path your attention takes before you argue with yourself. Use Rank The Capture Paths: count the cue, name the app or device, then rank the top risks by how often they override your own plan. Start with the highest-risk path and add one piece of friction.

ifThenPlans.context: Your thumb reaches for a feed during a routine pause.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the reach happens during a pause, then mark the cue in your tally and remove the phone path from the highest-ranked feed.

ifThenPlans.context: A useful platform is needed for a real task.
ifThenPlans.plan: If you need the platform, then write the purpose, session window, and exit condition before opening it.

ifThenPlans.context: Breaking news asks for another check before you can think.
ifThenPlans.plan: If a headline tries to pull you back, then put it on the slow-media list and read from a selected source later.

ifThenPlans.context: A work device keeps offering other rooms to wander through.
ifThenPlans.plan: If the device keeps opening side paths, then add one blocker, separate device, or single-purpose setup to the ranked path.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, count every reflex reach for a feed during your commute, first coffee, meals, and task handoffs. Record the cue and rank the top three capture paths by risk.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Run three spaced reps of Rank The Capture Paths this week. First, rank by frequency after one routine. Two days later, rank by risk across half a day. At week's end, add friction to the top path and check whether the count drops.

memorableLines.text: Defaults vote before you do.
Friction is a fence around chosen attention.
Purity can become another feed.
